newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin tackles economy, differs with NATO.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin tackles economy, differs with NATO.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin urged Russians on Tuesday to "Buy Russian" as part of a drive to revitalise the economy and install a new patriotic ideology to replace the old belief in communism.

At the same time, Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov was locked in closed-door bargaining with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana over what Russia sees as a threat to its role in the post-Cold War world -- NATO plans to expand eastwards.
The talks apparently failed to resolve remaining differences.
A brief Foreign Ministry statement said the two sides had come closer on some issues.
But it added: "Some difficult questions remain which must be resolved to pave the way for a mutually acceptable document on relations between Russia and NATO".
The latest round of talks between Primakov and Solana came one day before 66-year-old Yeltsin heads for talks in Germany with his friend, Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
The meeting, their second in three months, could be one of the toughest between the two men.
It is likely to focus on intensive efforts to negotiate a charter defining Russia's relationship with the NATO alliance as well as on bilateral economic ties.
Germany is Russia's biggest financial backer but it has been irritated by the Russian parliament's refusal to return a hoard of art treasures seized by the Red Army from the defeated Nazis.
Yeltsin's appeal for support for Russian produce, partly aimed at creating new jobs, was somewhat marred by a decision by Russia's Gazprom natural gas monopoly to shed 100,000 jobs this year.
The figure, a massive 26 percent of Gazprom's workforce, was thought to be the biggest single redundancy plan in Russia since market reforms started in 1992.
Yeltsin's radio address targeted the brightly-packaged imported goods which fill once-bare shop shelves across Russia.

"Is Russian chocolate worse than imported chocolate? No, it's better," he said. "And bread, sausage, dairy products and beer. Not to mention vodka! These goods are in no way inferior to imports and are often superior."
"When we buy domestic goods, we help our country, our Russian industry, we help ourselves. This is the sort of patriotism I like," Yeltsin said.
He said his "Buy Russian" campaign would help the economy, which officials say is on the point of growing again after seven years of severe recession.

"Do you want fewer unemployed? Do you want to help Russian enterprises? Do you want us to stand on our own feet and work at full strength? Then I say to you, buy our goods, our Russian goods, and you won't regret it," he said.
Yeltsin complained that Russia was flooded with promotions for foreign goods while domestic firms could not afford to advertise.
In a separate move aimed to help the cash-starved economy and overcome a stifling budget deficit, the government announced plans to issue a new dollar Eurobond.
A brief statement from First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said the dollar bond, running for at least five years, would be managed by investment banks JP Morgan and SBC Warburg.
Russia issued a heavily oversubscribed $1 billion five-year bond in November last year, and a well received two billion mark, seven-year bond in March this year.
